terra.problem: Saying Isaiah picked the word on purpose assigns him an intention the text does not state.
“That's why” gives a reason for the call to the whole earth that the passage does not explicitly state.
Being left unburied does not establish that there will be no funeral or that no one will come for the slain.
“I won't joke about it” comments on how Papa tells the passage. He can acknowledge that the line is heavy without discussing his own joking.
“Nothing up there gets left out” extends the statement beyond the stars and skies the passage names.
The lambs, goats and rams appear earlier in the same verse, not in the verse before it.
The explanation applies Zion's cause to both the day and the year. The text explicitly attaches it to the year of recompense.
The explanation says the day and the year are both for Zion's cause, though the text explicitly attaches that cause to the year of recompense.
The explanation ties both the day and the year to Zion's cause, though the text explicitly attaches that cause to the year of recompense.
The burnt-cookie joke makes light of the fire in a passage about devastating judgment. The comparison with an oven timer quitting is also unclear.
Calling the land simply empty overlooks the creatures Isaiah says will inhabit it.

“Once the people are gone” asserts that all the people have gone. The passage says no one will pass through and no nobles will be left, but does not say that.
The verse says no nobles will be left to proclaim a king, not that nobody at all will be left to name one.
The verse says no nobles will be left to proclaim a king. It does not say that no one at all is left to do so.
“Built to look strong” gives a purpose for the towers and fortresses that the text does not state.
The dropped-cookie joke is hard to follow: it is unclear why dropping a whole batch and losing track of three makes a coherent comparison to the creatures not going missing.
The text says no one will ever again pass through Edom. It does not say that no one is left to pass through.
